Code 
#Part 1

X1 = myData[['age']]
y = myData["charges"]
Code 
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X1,y, test_size =.2, random_state=321)
model1 = LinearRegression().fit(X_train,y_train)
y_pred_test1 = model1.predict(X_test)
Code 
intercept1 = model1.intercept_
coefs1 = model1.coef_
mse_test1 = mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_test1)
r_squared_test1 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred_test1)

print("Model 1 - age only PV")
print(f"intercept: {intercept1:.4f}")
print(f"age coefficient: {coefs1[0]:.4f}")
print(f"mse_test: {mse_test1:.4f}")
print(f"r_squared_test: {r_squared_test1:.4f}")
Model 1 - age only PV
intercept: 3782.5329
age coefficient: 217.5566
mse_test: 145557939.9188
r_squared_test: 0.0952

Interpretation: As age increases by 1 year, we see an increase in medical costs (charges), on average, of $230.07.

Out of all the models, it looks like the one that only had age and bmi did the best as it had the lowest MSE and highest R^2. As we increased the the degree of age, it looked to overfit the data by trying to adjust to follow the pattern of the scatterplot. More so, we saw a decrease in the test R^2. While traditionally the model would not decrease, this appliesto the predictive set. It could be the validation set was not explained well or the model did not do a good job handling unseen data.

    + geom_point(alpha=0.6, color='green')

           x='Predicted Charges',
           y='Residuals')
    + theme_classic()
)

(    ggplot(resid_df2, aes(x='predicted', y='residuals', color='blue'))
    + geom_point(alpha=0.6, color='Green')
    + geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype='dashed', color="gold")
    + labs(title='Residuals vs Predicted Charges (Model 1)',
           x='Predicted Charges',
           y='Residuals')
    + theme_classic()
)
